The selective response of the facets asks for a different explanation. Fluency and flexibility trade largely on retrieval speed and category switching, capacities that improve with practice in either condition, so it is unsurprising that they rose in both groups without a group difference 28 . Originality and elaboration depend instead on deeper transformation-combining remote associates, refining a concept until it holds together-and these operations draw on precisely the schema-building resources that germane load names 30 . On this reading the intervention did not make students think more; it changed the quality of thinking that the freed capacity could sustain, which is why the advantage concentrated in the two facets most sensitive to deep processing. The correlations in Fig. 7 sharpen that account. Fluency and flexibility hang together closely, as they should if both index the breadth of an initial search through memory, and their joint insensitivity to condition suggests that the generative toolchain did not simply accelerate idea retrieval. Originality and elaboration form a separate and more moderate pairing, and their weak association with fluency matters for interpretation: had originality risen only because students produced more responses, its correlation with fluency should have been considerably higher than the 0.41 observed. The same two-part structure has emerged from factor analyses of the Torrance battery, where fluency-driven and transformation-driven components separate rather than collapse into a single dimension 31 . Set against the long-run decline in originality and elaboration documented for large samples, the present result reads as a modest counterpoint, since the facets hardest to move historically are the ones this intervention moved 46 . Ulger's finding that creative training can lift divergent-thinking scores without touching problem-solving is a useful caution in the other direction: facet-level gains need not generalise to the wider construct 29 . The inverted-U finding for intrinsic load carries a caution that the earlier sections could only foreshadow. Too little intrinsic challenge leaves creative reasoning underpowered, while too much saturates working memory and crowds out the generative operations creativity needs 34 . The practical lesson is that intrinsic load should be tuned rather than minimised. A teacher designing an AIGC-supported animation task ought to calibrate conceptual difficulty toward the middle of the range-demanding enough to engage, restrained enough to leave room for exploration-rather than assuming that easier is always better 12 . This tempers a common but simplistic reading of load theory, and it is among the more transferable takeaways here. Set against prior work, these results are largely consonant but not identical. Studies pairing design thinking with germane load in STEAM settings likewise found creativity gains routed through deep engagement, which aligns with the mediation reported above 30 . The divergence lies in specificity: earlier flipped-learning and projectbased interventions reported broad creative-thinking improvement without partitioning which facets responded, so their apparent whole-scale gains may have masked the facet-level selectivity observed here 28 . Measurement grain is the likeliest reason for the discrepancy, since aggregating creativity into a single score can hide exactly the discriminant pattern that makes a mechanism legible 20 . Three implications follow for theory. The first concerns the status of germane load. Cognitive load theory has increasingly treated germane load as a redistribution of resources rather than an independent source of demand 14 , and the mediation estimate reported here gives that reconceptualisation an empirical foothold in a creative domain: germane load acted on originality and elaboration not directly but through a deep-processing strategy, which is what a redistribution account predicts. The second concerns the shape of the intrinsic-load effect. A curvilinear relation is hard to reconcile with the standard prescription to minimise load, and it suggests that the prescription was always domain-bound, holding for schema acquisition but not for tasks whose value lies in exploration. The third concerns creativity theory. Because the four facets responded differently to one instructional manipulation, treating divergent thinking as a single latent ability discards information that a facet-level model retains-an argument the creativity literature has long made on psychometric grounds 31 and that an intervention study can now make on experimental ones. For practice, the findings translate into three design rules rather than a general endorsement of generative tools. Assign generative assistance to the parts of a task that consume attention without building competence-formatting, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-77337-4 rendering, asset production-and keep it away from the parts where the struggle is the point. Make sure something recruits the freed capacity, because a lighter task is not automatically a more generative one; in the LTAC model the curation, evaluation, and reassembly demanded in the Thinking and Creating stages did that work. And calibrate conceptual difficulty toward the middle of the range instead of smoothing it away. For animation programmes weighing curricular reform, an open-source toolchain can lower barriers to production while raising the ceiling on deep creative work, but only where the instructional design treats load as something to shape rather than merely shed 32 . That conditional is the substantive message for anyone hoping to scale generative tools across higher education in art and design 3 . As accurately captured by Christodoulou and Zembylas23, technology acceptance is not a clear-cut matter of positive or negative attitudes but involves complicated stories and changes in relationships that affect the views and experiences of users. The present study attempts to address the gap in current literature on the lack of a comprehensive focus and understanding of the consequences of GenAI use on the “human side” of diverse cohorts of adult learners, particularly within the African/Ghanaian Taken together, findings from both the quantitative and qualitative phases paint a similar picture of how adult learners in the study perceive their DWB and QoL when interacting with GenAI. In the two phases of the study, adult learners' engagement with GenAI is characterised by coexisting gains and strain and not just a uniformly positive or negative experience. In the quantitative phase, DWB mean score was slightly above the 7-point Likert scale midpoint, with a meaningful minority of respondents reporting physical strain, and the composite mean of QoL indicated only modest gains in some aspects of GenAI-supported learning. The qualitative phase of the study throws further light on the mixed results in the survey; collaborators reflected on both appreciation for GenAI’s efficiency and anxiety over its encroachment on human creativity and authenticity. Using the unified ecological framework as a lens to understand the reciprocal and dynamic interrelationships between individuals, digital platforms, physical spaces, and macro-level factors, both findings highlight that adult learners’ DWB is a function of these interrelated factors. First, results from the survey and storytelling reveal that adult learners are knowledgeable of digital tools (including GenAI tools such as ChatGPT, DeepSeek, etc.) and, on average, possess digital skills and competencies which they use to interact meaningfully across several digital platforms (i.e. Google, learning management systems). items.abstract_text: Objective Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly integrated into university learning, raising questions about dependency-oriented reliance and self-regulation. Drawing on a self-regulated learning perspective, this study examined associations among GenAI dependency, effort regulation, and multidimensional perceived learning outcomes, including the statistical indirect association involving effort regulation. Methods Cross-sectional survey data were collected from 982 students at three higher education institutions in Guangdong Province, China. Confirmatory factor analysis and covariance-based structural equation modeling were conducted, with indirect associations tested using 5,000 bias-corrected bootstrap resamples. Sensitivity analyses adjusted for GenAI use frequency. Results The measurement model showed acceptable fit (CFI = 0.953, TLI = 0.944, RMSEA = 0.043, SRMR = 0.041). GenAI dependency showed a small negative total association with perceived learning outcomes ( β = −0.087) and was negatively associated with effort regulation ( β = −0.257). Effort regulation was positively associated with perceived learning outcomes ( β = 0.497). The residual direct association was nonsignificant ( β = 0.041), whereas the indirect association was negative and significant ( β = −0.128). After adjustment for GenAI use frequency, the indirect association remained significant, but the small total association was no longer significant. Conclusion The findings highlight effort regulation as a relevant learner-controlled process in the association between GenAI dependency and perceived learning outcomes. They also distinguish dependency-oriented reliance from frequency of GenAI use. The cross-sectional design and potential classroom clustering warrant cautious interpretation.

analysis.discussion: The present study examined the associations among generative AI dependency, effort regulation, and perceived learning outcomes among university students. GenAI dependency showed a small negative total association with perceived learning outcomes and was negatively associated with effort regulation, whereas effort regulation was positively associated with perceived learning outcomes. The overall negative association included a statistically significant negative indirect component involving effort regulation, while the residual direct association was small, positive in sign, and not statistically significant. The primary latent-variable model indicated a small negative total association between GenAI dependency and perceived learning outcomes. Although this association was statistically significant under the assumption of independent observations, its magnitude was limited ( β = −0.087), and the upper bound of its confidence interval was close to zero. The result therefore suggests only a modest relationship at the individual level and should not be interpreted as evidence of a substantial educational disadvantage associated with GenAI dependency. Moreover, because potential clustering within instructional classes was not accounted for, the precision of the estimated association may have been overstated. After effort regulation was included in the structural model, the residual direct association was not statistically significant. This pattern should not be interpreted as demonstrating that effort regulation fully explains the overall association or that the observed indirect association represents a causal mechanism. Previous research has associated GenAI dependency with procrastination, cognitive failures, poorer task performance, and weaker critical thinking ( Goh et al., 2025 ), while greater AI dependence has also been associated with lower critical thinking among university students ( Tian and Zhang, 2025 ). AI over-reliance has likewise been linked to less favorable learning performance ( Gao et al., 2026 ). However, these outcomes are not equivalent to perceived learning. The present study assessed students’ perceived cognitive, behavioral, and affective learning gains rather than objectively demonstrated achievement. Because perceived learning and independently assessed performance may diverge ( Deslauriers et al., 2019 ), the findings cannot establish whether GenAI dependency is similarly associated with objective learning outcomes. The present data cannot fully disentangle these subjective and objective dimensions, and the nonsignificant residual direct association should not be interpreted as evidence that GenAI dependency is educationally inconsequential. GenAI dependency was negatively associated with effort regulation, consistent with emerging evidence connecting AI dependency with self-regulatory functioning. Liu and Liu (2026) reported a negative association between metacognitive self-regulation and GenAI dependency, and Liu (2026) similarly identified a negative association between broader self-regulated learning and AI dependence among frequent AIGC users. More directly, Maizel et al. (2026) identified stronger effort regulation as being associated with lower AI dependency. In the present study, effort regulation was in turn positively associated with perceived learning outcomes, consistent with the role of persistence and resource management in academic functioning ( Pintrich, 2000 ; Waldeyer et al., 2022 ). These associations are particularly relevant in GenAI-supported learning because external assistance is readily available when academic work becomes difficult. Under such conditions, students’ capacity to sustain their own effort remains an important learner-controlled component of the learning process. The significant negative indirect association further indicates that GenAI dependency and perceived learning outcomes were statistically connected through effort regulation within the specified model. This association should be interpreted in light of the measures’ reference frames: GenAI dependency was specific to reliance on generative AI, whereas effort regulation reflected a broader academic self-regulatory tendency and perceived learning outcomes referred to recent coursework rather than a specific GenAI-supported task. The comparison of unadjusted and frequency-adjusted score-based models provided a more differentiated assessment of robustness. The negative association between GenAI dependency and effort regulation, the positive association between effort regulation and perceived learning outcomes, and the negative indirect association remained similar after adjustment for GenAI use frequency. However, the small negative total association was no longer statistically significant in the adjusted model, indicating that the evidence for this overall relationship was less robust. The change in the total coefficient was small and should not be interpreted as demonstrating that use frequency substantially explained the association. These results suggest that dependency-oriented reliance and frequency of GenAI use should be distinguished, but they do not establish their independent causal contributions to learning. Because the data were cross-sectional, the indirect association represents a statistical feature of the specified model rather than evidence of a causal mechanism. Reverse, reciprocal, and alternative directional relationships remain plausible. Moreover, the score-based sensitivity estimates should not be directly compared with the coefficients from the primary latent-variable SEM because the two approaches differ in their measurement specifications.
